utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Please be seated. Registrar, have the accused brought in, please. Please be seated.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Do the interpreters hear me? Good morning. Good morning to Prosecution and to Defence counsel, to the accused. Mr. Jelisic, do you feel all right this morning? Do you feel better?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I feel better, Your Honours, because I am taking some medication regularly. They are bringing it to me here.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] If you have a problem, do not hesitate, as always, to tell us, and then we'll deal with that problem. You may be seated now.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Let me turn to Mr. Nice, the Prosecutor. The floor is yours.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Your Honour, yesterday's witness was concluded. At the end of the session there was some slight uncertainty as to whether the Court had finished with the witness, but we understood that you had no further questions to ask of him, and in those circumstances, the next witness -- and indeed the next several witnesses -- will be taken by my learned friend Mr. Tochilovsky.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] You're right, Mr. Nice. It's very careful that you're watching over the proper conduct of the work by the Presiding Judge. It's true, I had forgotten to say that after this witness we -- well, I thought that I had merely said that the interpreters needed an extra break. All right. We're going to have Witness D brought in. Do we have a summary for Witness D, Mr. Prosecutor?

utterances.speaker: MR. TOCHILOVSKY
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. It was given to the Defence, and there is a -- we also have extra copies translated into French.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] When did you receive it, Mr. Greaves? Could you tell us when you received that? When were you given that summary?

utterances.speaker: MR. GREAVES
utterances.text: Shortly before Your Honours came in.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. All right then, I encourage you to read it carefully, and if you agree with certain points, you can say so. If not, you exercise the right to objections during your cross-examination.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Do you hear me? This is the Presiding Judge speaking to you. Do you hear me? This is a big room.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I can hear you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We're going to call you Witness D, because you have agreed to come on the condition that certain protective measures be taken for you in order to ensure your protection, and the Tribunal decided to grant those protective measures. Please remain standing as long as it takes to read the declaration which represents your oath on a piece of paper that the usher is going to give you in your own language. Please repeat what you see on that piece of paper.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. You may now be seated. We're going to show you a piece of paper and ask you to check to be sure that this is your name, but do not say your name. Simply nod to indicate that it is you, in fact. All right. This will now be given to the Defence, and to the Prosecution if the Prosecution wants it, and then to the Judges. From that point on, I believe that the -- I'm sure that the Prosecutor has explained to you how things are going to be conducted here. I'm asking you to be relaxed, be serene, calm. You're before a Tribunal, before Judges, and you are part of a trial which is being held against Mr. Jelisic, but be at ease, have no fear, speak without hatred, try to relax. The Office of the Prosecutor, through Mr. Tochilovsky, is going to start by asking you questions, and then of course you're going to be asked questions by the Defence counsel for the accused, but we haven't reached that point yet. Mr. Tochilovsky, you may proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOCHILOVSKY
utterances.text: Your Honour, before I start -- Your Honour, the witness didn't read the summary of his statements himself because he left his glasses at home. So the summary was read to him, and after it was read to him, he recognised the summary as correct. And I understand that the Defence has no objection if I lead the witness through the first four paragraphs, and then it will be in regular format.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] All right. If there are no objections from the Defence, we'll do as we did yesterday. We're going to admit as an exhibit the summary which was identified by Witness D. Do you have any comments, Mr. Greaves?

utterances.speaker: MR. GREAVES
utterances.text: No, Your Honour, thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. Thank you. Mr. Tochilovsky, please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOCHILOVSKY
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Just one small point. The witness can see without glasses, but he cannot read long text. His eyes get tired.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOCHILOVSKY
utterances.text: Mr. D, were you and your brother called from your house in Mujkici in Brcko and arrested by Serb forces on May 7, 1992?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOCHILOVSKY
utterances.text: Were you and two other men, including your brother, ordered to clear mines from a Muslim barricade in the street?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOCHILOVSKY
utterances.text: Were you moved then, with other people, from your neighbourhood to the Autunovic gas station?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOCHILOVSKY
utterances.text: Did another group join you at the gas station before you were all moved to the stadium?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOCHILOVSKY
utterances.text: Were you then put on buses and transported to Luka?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOCHILOVSKY
utterances.text: When did you arrive at Luka?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: 3.00 after midnight.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOCHILOVSKY
utterances.text: For how long were you held at Luka?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Eight days.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOCHILOVSKY
utterances.text: Did you see a man named Goran Jelisic at Luka?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [No translation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOCHILOVSKY
utterances.text: Can you describe the man? Can you give us his description?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I don't remember him very well. If I saw him in a uniform which he was wearing at the time, I would be able to recognise him.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOCHILOVSKY
utterances.text: Just tell us, what do you remember from his appearance?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: He was wearing a kind of a wrist band, and he had a pistol, a Scorpion, and he had a holster on his belt.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOCHILOVSKY
utterances.text: Did he carry anything else on him?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Occasionally, he also had a baton.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOCHILOVSKY
utterances.text: Was it always the same baton?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOCHILOVSKY
utterances.text: Did the person introduce himself to you?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. Yes, he did.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOCHILOVSKY
utterances.text: How did he introduce himself?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: "I am Goran Jelisic, also known as Adolf."

utterances.speaker: MR. TOCHILOVSKY
utterances.text: Did he express what is going to happen to Muslims and whether he is going to do anything to Muslims?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That as many balijas as possible should be killed.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOCHILOVSKY
utterances.text: Did he tell anything about what he is going to do in this regard?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOCHILOVSKY
utterances.text: What did he say?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, he just said that he would kill as many balijas as possible.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOCHILOVSKY
utterances.text: Did he ever mention the number of Muslims he already killed?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, he did.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOCHILOVSKY
utterances.text: What did he say?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: He twice said, "I killed two balijas, I killed three balijas."

utterances.speaker: MR. TOCHILOVSKY
utterances.text: Did you hear Jelisic giving orders to other camp personnel?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: He was in charge in the camp. He issued orders.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOCHILOVSKY
utterances.text: Were those prisoners who were taken from the hangar always returned back to the hangar?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Not always. They were taken outside. Some were returned, some were not.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOCHILOVSKY
utterances.text: Do you know what happened to those who didn't return?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: They were killed.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOCHILOVSKY
utterances.text: Did you hear any sounds after those prisoners were taken out and didn't return?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOCHILOVSKY
utterances.text: What kind of sounds?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: There were shots fired, using a silencer on the pistol.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOCHILOVSKY
utterances.text: How many prisoners were taken out of the hangar and never returned when you were in Luka?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I would say somewhere between 15 and 20 prisoners.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOCHILOVSKY
utterances.text: Do you remember the names of any of those prisoners, and just --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOCHILOVSKY
utterances.text: Were there any of your relatives among those?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOCHILOVSKY
utterances.text: Please don't mention any names of any of your relatives, but can you give us other names of those prisoners?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOCHILOVSKY
utterances.text: What other names?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Stipo, Jasce or Jasmin Curmurovic. His nickname was Jasce.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOCHILOVSKY
utterances.text: Please tell the Court, just in short, what happened to Jasce Curmurovic?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: On the 8th of May, he was taken out of the hangar about 4.00 or 5.00 in the afternoon and killed.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOCHILOVSKY
utterances.text: Who took him from the hangar?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Goran Jelisic.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOCHILOVSKY
utterances.text: Again, very shortly, can you tell the Court what happened to the man named Stipo?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: He was brought in at Luka on the 9th May in the morning. He was mistreated there. Then he was taken out and killed.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOCHILOVSKY
utterances.text: Was there anything unusual in Stipo's appearance when he was brought to the hangar?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: He was missing an ear. It had been cut off.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOCHILOVSKY
utterances.text: Who brought him to the hangar?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Goran and Kosta Simonovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOCHILOVSKY
utterances.text: How did they treat him?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: They were spitting on him. They abused him. They asked us who would volunteer to kill him, so nobody accepted and they killed him.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOCHILOVSKY
utterances.text: Can you tell the Court, again in short, what happened to Naza Bukvic in the camp?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: She was taken away on the 8th of May, between 11.00 and 12.00 in the evening, and they mistreated her until the morning. Then they brought her back, and they killed her sometime around 9.00 in the morning on the 9th of May.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOCHILOVSKY
utterances.text: Who mistreated her?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Goran, Kosta, and some other soldiers.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOCHILOVSKY
utterances.text: What kind of mistreatment was it?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: They beat her, they tortured her. They questioned her about her brother who had worked there with the police before the war.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOCHILOVSKY
utterances.text: Can you tell the Court what happened to her father, Muharem Ahmetovic?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: He was killed on the same day, but in the early evening, around 5.00 p.m. on the 9th of May.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOCHILOVSKY
utterances.text: Who took him from the hangar?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Goran.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOCHILOVSKY
utterances.text: Did he tell anything to this prisoner when he took him?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Ahmetovic asked where his daughter was, and Goran said, "You will find out shortly," and he saw her after half an hour or so. But they did not say anything else.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOCHILOVSKY
utterances.text: Did you see Goran kill a prisoner on May 9?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I did.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOCHILOVSKY
utterances.text: What did you see?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: My brother and two more prisoners were taking the body of a detainee who was killed there, and Goran took out another prisoner and shot him in the neck over the grate which was there.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOCHILOVSKY
utterances.text: Did Goran say anything to the prisoner before he shot him?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: He did.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOCHILOVSKY
utterances.text: What did he say?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: "No reason why to waste time with you," and then he killed him.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOCHILOVSKY
utterances.text: Please don't mention the name of your brother, but my question is what happened to your brother in the camp?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: He was killed on the 10th of May.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOCHILOVSKY
utterances.text: Who took him from the hangar?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Goran.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOCHILOVSKY
utterances.text: What did you hear shortly after your brother was taken from the hangar by Goran?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I heard a couple of shots made by a pistol with a silencer.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOCHILOVSKY
utterances.text: Witness D, did you carry bodies of prisoners in the camp?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I did.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOCHILOVSKY
utterances.text: How many bodies did you carry when you were in Luka?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: When I did that, there were about 15 or 20 bodies that were transported.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOCHILOVSKY
utterances.text: Were other detainees also called out to move the bodies?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: There were.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOCHILOVSKY
utterances.text: How many bodies did you see at the place where you took bodies?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Some 15 to 20 corpses.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOCHILOVSKY
utterances.text: Was it each time when you took bodies to that location?

utterances.speaker: MR. TOCHILOVSKY
utterances.text: I think the interpreters didn't hear the answer.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOCHILOVSKY
utterances.text: Can you repeat your answer?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOCHILOVSKY
utterances.text: What kind of wounds did those bodies have?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Firearm wounds.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOCHILOVSKY
utterances.text: Do you know how those bodies were taken from the camp?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: They were taken away in the refrigerated truck of Bimeks.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOCHILOVSKY
utterances.text: How often did you see the Bimeks truck coming to the camp?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Once a day.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOCHILOVSKY
utterances.text: Can you describe the truck? What was the colour of the truck?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It was painted blue and white, and it had the inscription "Bimeks" on it. Sometimes it was a two-ton, sometimes it was a three-ton truck.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOCHILOVSKY
utterances.text: May I have the assistance of the usher to place Prosecution Exhibit 4 before the witness. Just the left upper corner on the screen, the left upper. Lower. A little bit more. Lower, more lower. Yes, that is okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOCHILOVSKY
utterances.text: Witness D, can you see a truck in the left upper corner of this picture?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOCHILOVSKY
utterances.text: Is that the type of truck you saw in Luka?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. It was also painted blue on its sides, and there is also an inscription "Bimeks".

utterances.speaker: MR. TOCHILOVSKY
utterances.text: It was white on the rear side, as it is on the picture?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOCHILOVSKY
utterances.text: Thanks.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOCHILOVSKY
utterances.text: Your Honours, before I ask the witness the next questions, I would respectfully ask you to move into private session, because the questions I have to ask are related to his identity.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] All right. We'll move into private session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: 9 (redacted) 10 (redacted) 11 (redacted) 12 (redacted) 13 (redacted) 14 (redacted) 15 (redacted) 16 (redacted) 17 (redacted) 18 (redacted) 19 (redacted) 20 (redacted) 21 (redacted) 22 (redacted) 23 (redacted) 24 (redacted) 25 (redacted) 1 (redacted) 2 (redacted) 3 (redacted) 4 (redacted) 5 (redacted) 6 (redacted) 7 (redacted) 8 (redacted) 9 (redacted) 10 (redacted) 11 (redacted) 12 (redacted) 13 (redacted) 14 (redacted) 15 (redacted) 16 (redacted) 17 (redacted) 18 (redacted) 19 (redacted) 20 (redacted)

utterances.speaker: MR. TOCHILOVSKY
utterances.text: With regard to the list on page 1 of Exhibit 12, there is the name of Ahmetovic, Muharem. Is that the Ahmetovic, Muharem you just mentioned as killed in Luka?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOCHILOVSKY
utterances.text: On the same page, there is the name Glavocevic, Stipo. Is that the same person you mentioned as Stipo killed in Luka?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOCHILOVSKY
utterances.text: On the second page of this list there is the name -- in the middle of the list, there is the name Jukic Sadik. Do you know anything about his fate?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: He was killed at home.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOCHILOVSKY
utterances.text: Do you know the circumstances of this killing?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOCHILOVSKY
utterances.text: You did not see the killing?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOCHILOVSKY
utterances.text: You just heard about it?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOCHILOVSKY
utterances.text: Page 3 of the same exhibit, in the middle of the list, there is the name Muranjkovic, Galib. Do you know about the fate of this person?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: He was killed too.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOCHILOVSKY
utterances.text: Where was he killed?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: In Luka, after I left.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOCHILOVSKY
utterances.text: So you did not see the killing, but you were told by someone else?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: His brother told me.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOCHILOVSKY
utterances.text: On the same page, Pezerovic, Suljo. Do you know what happened to him?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: He was killed in Luka too.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOCHILOVSKY
utterances.text: How do you know that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: He was killed after I left, and I was told that by those who were exchanged after me.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOCHILOVSKY
utterances.text: On the bottom of this list, the name Residovic, Enver; what do you know about this person?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: He was killed at home.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOCHILOVSKY
utterances.text: Do you know the circumstances in which he was killed?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOCHILOVSKY
utterances.text: Page 4 of the exhibit, at the end of the list, there are three names of Tursunovic. Sefket: Have you heard about this person, what happened to him?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: He was killed at home.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOCHILOVSKY
utterances.text: Did you see that killing?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOCHILOVSKY
utterances.text: Tursunovic, Zekerija?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: He was in Luka, was released, and was killed in his home.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOCHILOVSKY
utterances.text: Tursunovic, Zijad, on the same page?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That is his son. He was also in Luka, then released, and then killed at home.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOCHILOVSKY
utterances.text: But you didn't see the killing, did you?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOCHILOVSKY
utterances.text: Next is Exhibit 13. On the first page of this exhibit, Hodzic, Ahmed, or Papa. Do you know about his fate?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: He was a businessman. He had a shop, and he was killed in front of the police station.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOCHILOVSKY
utterances.text: Did you see the killing, or you were told about that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I heard about it. I was told about it.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOCHILOVSKY
utterances.text: Next name, on the same page, Husein Kaknjo.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: He was the manager of a company. He was retired, but I do not know what happened to him.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOCHILOVSKY
utterances.text: Next page of the same list, Suljevic, Hamdija?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. He was killed at home.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOCHILOVSKY
utterances.text: Did you see that, or you heard that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I heard it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Excuse me, I don't quite see the name on the next page. Could you make it more clear to me, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOCHILOVSKY
utterances.text: The name is -- it's number 13 -- no, it's not. Yes, it's Number 13. Suljevic, Hamdija. So I will refer to numbers rather than to the page.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOCHILOVSKY
utterances.text: The next number is 17, Sakib Edhemovic.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: A prominent surgeon. He was killed in Brcko.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOCHILOVSKY
utterances.text: Number 36, Osman Vatic. Do you know what happened to this person?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: He was a lawyer and was killed in Brcko.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOCHILOVSKY
utterances.text: Did you see what happened, or you just heard about it?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I only heard about it.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOCHILOVSKY
utterances.text: I have no further questions, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. Tochilovsky, for the concise way that you conducted your examination of the witness. I encourage Mr. Greaves, naturally, to tell us approximately how much time he is going to need for his cross-examination, and I go back to 90(H), which says that the cross-examination must deal with the examination-in-chief or with the credibility of the witness. Mr. Greaves, you may proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. GREAVES
utterances.text: Thank you. Can I just alert Your Honour to this: You'll see that I'm wearing glasses today. I have a considerable problem with my right eye today, and I'm in some pain. There may come a time when I have to ask to go and see a doctor. I'm going to struggle on for the moment, but I'm in some difficulties at the moment, and I'm not very comfortable.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] If you have to see a doctor, please tell us, and I certainly hope that it isn't going to be very serious. We really are having a lot of problems with glasses today. Mr. Greaves, please continue.

utterances.speaker: MR. GREAVES
utterances.text: Mr. G [sic], I want to ask you, please, about your -- perhaps we can go into private session at this stage, please?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] This is not Witness G, but rather D.

utterances.speaker: MR. GREAVES
utterances.text: I'm sorry. Perhaps we could go into private session, please, for the first questions that I have to ask.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, of course. Let's go into a private session for the first questions. Let me remind you, of course, that these are generally public sessions, but please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. GREAVES
utterances.text: I want to ask you now, please, Mr. D, about the 30th of April, 1992. That was a date when I think some bridges were blown in Brcko over the River Sava. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GREAVES
utterances.text: Is this also right, that on that day you heard something on the radio, some sort of ultimatum that was being issued?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No. I heard that on the 1st of May.

utterances.speaker: MR. GREAVES
utterances.text: I'm sorry, it's not clear from the summary when it is you were saying that was what you had heard.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: 1st of May.

utterances.speaker: MR. GREAVES
utterances.text: Who was it who gave the ultimatum? Can you identify that person?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: They were the leadership of the SDS.

utterances.speaker: MR. GREAVES
utterances.text: So there was more than one person who gave this ultimatum on the radio?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GREAVES
utterances.text: Can you put any names to any of those people who were on the radio, giving this ultimatum?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. GREAVES
utterances.text: What was the nature of the ultimatum, Mr. D?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: To turn in the weapons or else the town would be shelled. In other words, that the Muslims surrender the weapons.

utterances.speaker: MR. GREAVES
utterances.text: I want to ask you about this, please:

utterances.speaker: MR. GREAVES
utterances.text: Your Honour, strictly speaking, this isn't a matter which arises out of examination in chief. Your Honour won't have details of this, but it relates to somebody who was taken into the military forces. I want to ask about the consequences of what might have happened to that person had he not gone into the forces.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, but so long as the Prosecutor has the chance to retort to that, Mr. Greaves, and so long as it doesn't take too much time. I remind you that you haven't told us how much time you're going to be using.

utterances.speaker: MR. GREAVES
utterances.text: Your Honour, I think about two hours in all, but I hope to be less than that. But I'm not sure I can keep it any shorter than that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I am simply asking you to go as quickly and as concisely as you can. You can set your time as you like. I don't have the power to control what you're doing in your cross-examination, but I can insist that you remain within the limits of the examination in chief, though I do agree with my colleagues, with whom I've consulted, we agree that you can go outside of the examination in chief. But I want you to respect strictly a proper amount of time in order to conduct your cross-examination. All right. Ask your question now, Mr. Greaves.

utterances.speaker: MR. GREAVES
utterances.text: Mr. D, I don't want to know the name of your relation, but I think that in early May 1992, a relation of yours was called up into the Serb armed forces. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. GREAVES
utterances.text: Your Honour, I don't want to mention the name in open session, but he said, "No." But obviously I'm asking it for a reason. Can we go into closed session briefly so that I can remind him of what I suggest the name is?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. Yes, all right. Private session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: 23 (redacted) 24 (redacted) 25 (redacted)

utterances.speaker: MR. GREAVES
utterances.text: Mr. D, we've established and I've refreshed your memory as to who we're talking about. Were you aware of the circumstances in his being summoned to the Serbian army?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GREAVES
utterances.text: Did you know at that time what the consequences would have been for him had he failed to answer the summons to join the army?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: He would have been killed. He was forced.

utterances.speaker: MR. GREAVES
utterances.text: So was that well known at the time, that those would have been the consequences, that if you had not joined, not done as you were told, you would have been liable to be killed; that was well known, was it?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GREAVES
utterances.text: I want to ask you now, please, Mr. D, about the barricade which you were asked to go and deal with after your detention. Was that at a particular petrol station in Brcko?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GREAVES
utterances.text: You had been arrested by soldiers. Were they soldiers in uniform of the JNA?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. Some were wearing uniforms, and then some others were without uniforms.

utterances.speaker: MR. GREAVES
utterances.text: How many of the people in your neighbourhood were arrested at the same time?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Somewhere around 20.

utterances.speaker: MR. GREAVES
utterances.text: Was it that group of 20 that was forced to go to the petrol station?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GREAVES
utterances.text: Was the barricade a barricade which had been established by Muslim forces or by Serb forces?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Muslim.

utterances.speaker: MR. GREAVES
utterances.text: Were the things that you had to remove from the barricade, were they actually placed in the barricade, or were they in a basement of the building, or what actually had to be removed?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Anti-tank mines from the barricade.

utterances.speaker: MR. GREAVES
utterances.text: The soldiers who were supervising this exercise, were they from all parts of the former Yugoslavia?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GREAVES
utterances.text: What about the civilians who were with you, who were part of these Serbian forces; were they local people or from all over Yugoslavia?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, from throughout the former Yugoslavia.

utterances.speaker: MR. GREAVES
utterances.text: Help me with this, please: When you were at the petrol station, was there any fighting that you could hear taking place in the Brcko district?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. GREAVES
utterances.text: Was there any sign that there had been fighting prior to your arrival at the petrol station, any fighting at that location?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GREAVES
utterances.text: Was that in the form of damage or in the form of signs that people had been injured or killed?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Just damage.

utterances.speaker: MR. GREAVES
utterances.text: During the course of the 7th of May elsewhere in Brcko, did you see signs of fighting which had previously taken place?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: You could hear the shooting coming from the town.

utterances.speaker: MR. GREAVES
utterances.text: During the course of the 7th of May, did you see any signs of people who had been killed or wounded as a result of that fighting?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. GREAVES
utterances.text: Is this right, that you were then joined up with by other groups of people?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GREAVES
utterances.text: You were taken to some sort of stadium, a sports stadium or something like that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GREAVES
utterances.text: Firstly, please, will you help us with this? How many people were you joined up with before you went to the stadium?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I'd say about ten.

utterances.speaker: MR. GREAVES
utterances.text: When you got to the stadium, were there people already there who had been detained?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GREAVES
utterances.text: How many people were already there?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Somewhere about 20.

utterances.speaker: MR. GREAVES
utterances.text: Is this correct, that you were taken from there, during the course of the night, to Luka?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: We were taken to Luka in the evening, but we were brought to the stadium in the afternoon.

utterances.speaker: MR. GREAVES
utterances.text: Yes. Well, just give us the time at which you got to the stadium?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Somewhere around 5.00.

utterances.speaker: MR. GREAVES
utterances.text: It was during the hours of darkness that you were taken to Luka?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GREAVES
utterances.text: At what time did you arrive at Luka?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Some three hours after midnight.

utterances.speaker: MR. GREAVES
utterances.text: Amongst the people who had been detained at the stadium, had more come in before you were taken? In other words, more people arrived after you arrived?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. GREAVES
utterances.text: What was the total of people that were taken from the stadium to Luka, in approximate terms?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Somewhere around 35 persons, approximately.

utterances.speaker: MR. GREAVES
utterances.text: Were those all men, or were they a mixture of men and women?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: There were also women and children.

utterances.speaker: MR. GREAVES
utterances.text: I'd like to ask you this, please: In your statement to the Office of the Prosecutor, you give a description of the camp itself, or the facility at Luka, and you describe one particular building which is an office building. Do you recall the office building?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GREAVES
utterances.text: Is that a building that was used by the camp commander?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: This was a customs house, or office, and it was used by the camp commander.

utterances.speaker: MR. GREAVES
utterances.text: And are you able to help us as to who -- describe the camp commander to us?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Goran Jelisic was presenting himself as the camp commander.

utterances.speaker: MR. GREAVES
utterances.text: I want to ask you now about --

utterances.speaker: MR. GREAVES
utterances.text: I'm sorry, Your Honour. Just give me a moment, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. GREAVES
utterances.text: Just one aspect of the layout of the camp, of the facility. Is this right, that behind the hangars in which you were detained there is first of all a railroad and then the Sava River?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GREAVES
utterances.text: How far from the hangars is the Sava River, in your estimation?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Somewhere around 20 metres.

utterances.speaker: MR. GREAVES
utterances.text: Having arrived at the camp, were you all put into the same place, or were you separated in some way?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: All in the same place.

utterances.speaker: MR. GREAVES
utterances.text: And was that in the first warehouse, the first hangar of the buildings opposite the administration offices?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GREAVES
utterances.text: Is this right, Mr. D, that on the morning of the 8th of May, the morning after you were taken to the Luka facility, the women and children were separated from you and handed over to the Red Cross?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GREAVES
utterances.text: Separated by the officials at the camp?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GREAVES
utterances.text: And handed over to the safety and care of the Red Cross?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GREAVES
utterances.text: Is this right, that the group of people who had been gathered at the stadium and then taken to Luka were all Muslims?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GREAVES
utterances.text: And it follows from that that all of the women and children who were separated from you and handed over to the Red Cross by officials at the camp were all Muslim?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Greaves, perhaps take a 20-minute break. All right?

utterances.speaker: MR. GREAVES
utterances.text: Your Honour, I wonder whether you would perhaps make that half an hour, please, because I -- first of all, I need to see my client; but I'm not feeling very well, I have to tell you. I've got a very, very bad headache, and I'm feeling most uncomfortable, and I would just like a break of that kind, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] All right. We'll take a half hour.

utterances.speaker: MR. GREAVES
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] And if you need, we can break until 12.00, not resume until 12.00.

utterances.speaker: MR. GREAVES
utterances.text: No, if you give me half an hour, it's going to help. I just want to sit down and -- thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Perhaps Hirad can remain in contact with the Defence to see whether, after a half hour, he can resume. All right, we'll take our break now.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We'll resume the hearing now. Registrar, have the accused brought in, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Londrovic, could you tell the Trial Chamber exactly what is happening with your colleague?

utterances.speaker: MR. LONDROVIC
utterances.text: Your Honours, the only information I have is that something is wrong with Mr. Greaves's right eye, and something is wrong with the lens. And Your Honours accorded us a break of half an hour, but Mr. Greaves did not feel well, and he went to see a doctor, and the latest news that I have is that he had gone to the doctor, but he did not call again. Your secretary tried. I gave his telephone number at home, and his wife answered; he had not called home either. I suppose that Mr. Greaves has gone to the hospital because his doctor was not in his private surgery. I thought that he would appear here. I really did not think that he would not turn up by now, by 10 to 3.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] With regrets that Mr. Greaves could not contact the Registrar, definitely, have you heard no news?

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Well, a few moments ago, Mr. Greaves did contact the Registry and told us that he would not be available this afternoon.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Londrovic, will you be able to substitute for Mr. Greaves during the end of these cross-examinations? This has already happened several times. Can you substitute for your colleague?

utterances.speaker: MR. LONDROVIC
utterances.text: Your Honours, with all due respect to your time and the time of our learned friends from the Prosecution and everybody else in this courtroom, I should like to ask you to postpone the cross-examination envisaged for this afternoon. Yes, I did work with Mr. Greaves, but we never thought that we would be faced with this situation. So I should indeed like to ask you, if possible at all, to postpone the resumption of this cross-examination until tomorrow morning at 10.00. If Mr. Greaves feels unwell tomorrow, then of course, I shall take over the cross-examination.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. Londrovic. Under those conditions, if we are sure that you will be able to replace Mr. Greaves tomorrow, I guess that would perhaps be all right. Turning to the Prosecutor, can you bring in the next witness for the examination-in-chief? Perhaps that would be the best thing to do, unless we were to give you a half hour in order to go get him.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: No, I think we are probably in a position to call him in very swiftly. The only thing that remains to be done with that next witness is for him to consider a version of the summary and to approve it or, alternatively, to note corrections on it. The preparation of summaries has been quite meticulous, but even with all sorts of earlier preparations, the translation department finds it very difficult to provide updated translations of earlier draft documents. If you would permit our case manager to go outside for a minute, she can find out how many minutes it would take for the next witness to be ready to give his evidence in chief. We can probably avoid a short adjournment now if you would permit her to do that. While she is doing that, could I raise another topic? Because even if we take that witness in chief, I don't think that will consume the totality of the afternoon, and I don't know whether Mr. Londrovic is ready immediately to cross-examine that witness. I would hope he is, but it may be that he isn't. To deal with the possibility that there will be some spare time this afternoon, can I explain what the position is about one of our expert witnesses, the one who would be coming from Australia? I asked Mr. Greaves whether he could give consideration to explaining to me what was in issue between him and that witness, and indeed, I suggested to him if there was anything he would like the witness to explain, by all means, he could telephone the witness in Australia, of course at our expense, and see if he could obtain help from the witness in that way. In the event, Mr. Greaves has been good enough to explain to me that there is only one issue concerning that witness. The witness's name is Wright, and he deals with exhumation of a mass grave. And the Defence, as I am informed, are going to argue that one particular paragraph of the report -- it's paragraph 9 -- is inadmissible from this particular witness. Well, now, of course, in order to discuss issues of admissibility, the Chamber has to have some -- probably some detailed knowledge of what it is that the witness would be led by us to give in evidence, and accordingly, it would be necessary for the Tribunal to consider to some degree the report of Mr. Wright to know what's going to be argued. And it had occurred to me as potentially a useful use of this afternoon's time to distribute to the Court the report of Mr. Wright, which is available in English and French, and to invite you at least to look at paragraph 9 of it, in order that we could argue the admissibility of that paragraph this week; today or tomorrow. Once it's been resolved as it could be, whether the paragraph is admissible or not, or whether it's only admissible on certain terms, then I'll be able to make the decision whether it's necessary to call the witness from Australia or not, and of course if it's not necessary to call him, for whatever reason, his report can be read with very considerable saving of time and money. So may I, at some stage this afternoon, distribute to Your Honours, in whatever language you would prefer, this report and invite you to consider it, at least as far as paragraph 9 is concerned. I'm told, incidentally, that the witness needs another 15 minutes to peruse the summary, and so can I say a little bit more about the report to explain, without arguing the point one way or another, what paragraph 9 is about. The witness, Professor Wright, I think it's a professor, with representatives of the Office of the Prosecution, examined the mass grave outside Brcko and is able to give clear and, it appears, unchallenged evidence of the findings of bodies in four of the graves, and indeed he's able to derive conclusions about the movement of bodies from the grave after the bodies were first laid there and matters of that sort. In paragraph 9, he deals with the findings of both bricks and masonry that was found on a layer above the bodies in certain places, and he draws certain conclusions from the nature of masonry found, in particular the cut angles of particular bits of masonry, which are consistent with having come from a mosque, and there's another piece of masonry that is plainly of Muslim origin. So that's the paragraph. It's of some significance to the Prosecution, because it would, as it were, be heaping insult on injury, not only to cover a mass grave with something but to cover it with the masonry of a destroyed mosque. So it's not an irrelevant or immaterial piece of evidence, but it's something about which the Defence wish to argue. So if I can distribute the document, and if the Chamber has some time this afternoon to consider at least that paragraph, then we'll be well poised to argue admissibility, and I'll be able, before the weekend, to decide whether that witness need be troubled to come all the way from Australia.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I understand what you've said. I understand, Mr. Nice. But does this have anything to do with admissibility? It seems to me that what you've said has more to do with the amount of weight to be given to this or that passage in the report. But as regards admissibility as an exhibit, does that play a role? You are speaking about things which are being challenged, but does this prevent the admission of the material as an exhibit, even if further on the Defence were to contest it, contest it either by demanding that the witness arrive or by other means?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Your Honour, of course I will be arguing that the answer to that question is "No" and indeed it doesn't affect admissibility, but I can't really judge the strength or power of my learned friend's argument to exclude when he makes it. I'm simply using the available time to set the scene, and I can't present argument further at this stage. I must wait for Mr. Greaves, or maybe Mr. Londrovic could advance the arguments they wish to advance.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I think that we're going to wait until we see the article, the report, but I think that's really a question of substance and weight to be given to that paragraph 9. Since I don't have it in front of me, I can't say anything more. If you agree, it's now 3.00, I suggest we adjourn until 3.30. But at 3.30, we will hear the next witness, that is, the examination in chief, and we'll ask Mr. Londrovic to prepare himself for conducting the cross-examination, then to use the time that he has until 5.30, assuming that the Prosecution has finished before that. It's now 3.00. I think that will give you enough time for the witness, that is, 30 minutes, and during that time you will be sure that you give us the reports. You will distribute the report; is that correct, Mr. Nice?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: The French, English, or both?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Theoretically, I would have a slight preference for the French version, but if you would really prefer I read it in English, I'll somehow manage, but it will take a little longer. But you're very kind. As far as I'm concerned, I would prefer to have it in French.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: It will come to Your Honour in French.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Perhaps the usher can distribute it. It's very kind of you, and I think that you've given us some work for the next half hour, though I ask the registrar to give us the report as we go out during this forced adjournment. All right. We will adjourn until 3.30.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: Can I have it in the two languages to check the translation?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Very well.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] And Judge Rodrigues would prefer it, who does not have a Portuguese version here since it's not an official version, he would prefer it in French as well, and that way we can check both versions. Thank you very much, Judge Riad. Mr. Londrovic, excuse me, I thought that you had agreed with everything that had been taken up, but perhaps you aren't. Excuse me for interrupting you.

utterances.speaker: MR. LONDROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I should only like to respond to what Mr. Nice has said. From what I learned from Mr. Greaves with regard to this expert statement, the Defence objects against I believe it is paragraph 9. But as it was in English, I had no opportunity of reading it in our language, so I haven't read it. But Mr. Greaves enjoys my full trust. The Defence objects to one part of the statement. As my learned friend from the Prosecution correctly said, it concerns this building material, this masonry which the witness claims comes from a mosque. So we, however, decided to agree with the Prosecution and not to ask this witness to come. We also suggested that if they agree to strike out this part of the statement which we find contention, then we shall agree to the rest of the statement, and we shall also accept that the witness -- and we shall also not insist on calling this witness. If the Prosecution, however, does not want to strike this part from the statement, if I understood Mr. Greaves properly, then we shall be objecting to this statement, and we shall also want to cross-examine that witness with regard to some of the circumstances and things in that statement. I should also like to add something else, if I may. Of course, I'm not objecting against examination in chief of the next witness, and then I hope we shall have a break, and if Mr. Greaves is not ready tomorrow, then I shall take over the cross-examination. But will you please allow me not to begin with the cross-examination of any witness today?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] As regards the first point, I don't think we can say anything further until the Judges have read it. As regards the second request, the Judges will take a decision at the proper time. But let me remind you that the Defence works together. The accused has two counsel, and both of the counsel are interchangeable, theoretically. At least you should be able to organise yourself in that manner. In circumstances when Mr. Greaves began a cross-examination, we will not force you to continue with it. That seems clear, and in fact we've already said that to you. But as regards the rest, there has to be some reason for having two counsel, two lawyers, Mr. Londrovic. Therefore, perhaps today it would be useful for you to work with your client, who is going to need you even more than he might on another day. Perhaps he won't need you to do it, perhaps it won't be very long either, but I do ask that you prepare yourself should the cross-examination take place today. All right. We're going to adjourn now until 3.30.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We will now resume the hearing. Have the accused brought in, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Greaves, we are very pleased to see you back. How do you feel?

utterances.speaker: MR. GREAVES
utterances.text: Your Honour, the position is this. I went first of all this morning to the main hospital in the centre of The Hague. In due course, they sent me on to the eye specialist hospital at Leijenburg, which is on the outskirts of The Hague, and I was seen by an eye specialist at that hospital. I have had a -- diagnosed an eye infection which may or may not spread to my left eye. I have been given some treatment for it in the form of an antibiotic ointment. That has left me in the situation where I cannot see properly out of my right eye at all at the present time. I do not feel fit enough to continue cross-examining the witness that I started cross-examining this morning. I hope Your Honours will understand that. It's obviously a considerable regret to me that that's happened, but I fear that that nature sometimes has a way of making difficulties for all of us. What I would ask Your Honour to be able to do -- and I understand from my learned friend Mr. Nice that the witness has now been sent back to his hotel -- is to be able to resume, in due course, his cross-examination. I've been told by the doctor that if there is no improvement in my eye, I have to return to the hospital tomorrow morning; but of course I hope that I shall feel better then and will be able to resume. Your Honour, I have only recently returned, and I have had a brief conversation with my learned colleague, Mr. Londrovic. I understand that the proposition at the moment is this. The next witness, who has not yet been examined in chief, should come and be examined in chief, and as I understand it, the initial proposal was that my learned friend should cross-examine him. May I please address Your Honour about the second of those two propositions? We have no difficulty with the idea that Your Honour should hear the evidence in chief of the next witness, but the way in which the defence of Mr. Jelisic has been organised is such that we complement each other in the tasks that we undertake. There are many tasks that Mr. Londrovic undertakes which are things that I simply couldn't begin to undertake at all. Conversely, there are tasks which have been delegated to me, which are tasks that have been delegated to me because of my experience in the English criminal courts, and, in particular, as you will have seen, I have been delegated the task of cross-examining each witness, and I have prepared the cross-examination of each witness. We would respectfully ask that whilst we have absolutely no objection to the proposition that you should hear the evidence in chief of the next witness, that the tasks having been delegated in that way, we should be allowed to organise our defence -- continue to organise our defence in the way in which we have been planning for many months now, and that Mr. Londrovic should not be forced into a situation where, without having prepared a cross-examination, Your Honour should force him to do that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Nice, what is your opinion about this? Because this is causing a great many difficulties. And I would like to remind you, Mr. Greaves, that the Rules say that I must avoid all needless consumption of time. And as you were not here before, and you didn't perhaps know that Mr. Londrovic had accepted the suggestion of the Tribunal, but your being here shows us that even though you cannot see everything through your eyes, your mind is very lively, and you've even understood Mr. Londrovic's position. But before the Judges change their position, we would like to hear what the Prosecutor has to say. Mr. Nice, this case is becoming very delicate, and I would like justice to be conducted within this Tribunal in the proper way. The presence of two attorneys is a right which is acknowledged in the Tribunal for each accused; some even have three counsel or even more. But of course it is self-evident that for the OTP, the defence is indivisible, as is the Office of the Prosecutor. One must be prepared, and I believe that we are trying to facilitate the Defence's work. Mr. Nice, you will bring in the next witness, and then you will conduct the examination-in-chief. About how much time are you going to need?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: 40 minutes. Between 40 minutes and one hour, I would have thought. We are obviously very concerned about the recent course of events, having in mind that we are still calling witnesses who were called on a previous occasion and then not reached, for want of time, and detained in The Hague for either one or two weekends. I summoned eight witnesses last weekend, forecasting, as has proved to be the case, that it would be possible to deal with the examination-in-chief in a very compact way. And I think the first witness took under two hours -- one hour and 40 minutes -- actually in the witness box, of which a significant proportion was devoted to the lists which were dealt with at the request of the Defence. I think the second witness in chief was well under an hour, and I think Your Honour may have mentioned 35 or 45 minutes, and likewise the last witness, at the dextrous hands of Mr. Tochilovsky, was about half an hour or a little more. We have five witnesses, brought here before last weekend, still to go, so we are very concerned at the possibility of further time being taken which would be properly used if both counsel were able to cross-examine. And I have noticed that Mr. Greaves has at all times referred to Mr. Londrovic as the lead counsel, and it is astonishing to think that either counsel, but certainly the lead counsel, should not in principle be in a position to perform one of the fundamental tasks of defence counsel in this Tribunal. So with all respect for and understanding of the problems faced by the Defence, we would press the Court to require that the examination and cross-examination of these witnesses continues as soon as possible, and not later than tomorrow morning.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Would you like to respond to that, Mr. Greaves? But please don't repeat what you've already said.

utterances.speaker: MR. GREAVES
utterances.text: I won't. I was simply going to say to Your Honour that I think I've set out what the position is. Of course, my learned friend Mr. Londrovic wasn't expecting to have to cross-examine someone. He hasn't prepared a cross-examination for the next witness. Preparing such a cross-examination takes several hours, and I tend to sit up into the early hours of the morning preparing matters, and it's not something that necessarily one can do just at the click of one's fingers. That, I'm sure, Your Honour having been associated with the courts for a long time, will appreciate only too well, what the position is when you have to deal with something like that unexpectedly. Of course, it's desirable, if one can, if one was in the best of all possible worlds, one can take things up immediately, but the reality is my learned friend has not prepared himself for that situation. No doubt, if he has the notice of overnight, he could prepare in contingency for cross-examining the next witness tomorrow morning, but I hope that I will be here and able to do that. I hope that assists Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Who is the lead counsel for the Defence team? Is it you, Mr. Londrovic? Who is the lead counsel, if there is a lead counsel?

utterances.speaker: MR. LONDROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, there is no lead or boss in our team. We work collectively.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I congratulate you. You know, when one has lead counsel or chiefs, it's always a tricky business, how he can designate a chief. I would like first, however, to speak with my colleagues.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The Trial Chamber Judges, confronted with this exceptional situation of the fact that the cross-examination could not be conducted by Mr. Greaves, rule as follows in this case: They would first like to recall the principle which they draw from Rule 90(G). That is, the Trial Chamber shall exercise control over the mode of interrogating witnesses and presenting evidence so as only to make it effective and to avoid the needless consumption of time. The Judges would also like to assert that respect which is owed to the witness is basic, especially under these circumstances, that this trial has already been interrupted on several occasions for different reasons. Under these conditions, the Judges take from these principles the obligation for Mr. Londrovic to conduct the cross-examination. Nonetheless, exceptionally and for the twofold reason that in any case this afternoon is already almost over, neither Mr. Londrovic nor Mr. Greaves could know in advance the Judges' position in this Trial Chamber in a difficult case where one of the members could not be present -- I'm not speaking about the Office of the Prosecutor -- in a case where he could not carry out the case that was assigned to him. Exceptionally, the Judges have decided that this afternoon will be devoted to the examination in chief, and then afterwards the Court will adjourn until tomorrow morning. Lastly, the Judges would like to point out, both to the Prosecution and to the Defence, that in the future, any inability on the part of one of the members of either office must be immediately corrected by substituting the other member of the team. Therefore, it's in consideration of the fact that you were not informed that exceptionally the Judges are granting your request, Mr. Greaves, and under these conditions we can now move to the examination in chief of the following witness. At 9.00 tomorrow morning, either Mr. Londrovic or Mr. Greaves will conduct both the cross-examinations which will not have been done after the examination in chief of Witness D and the cross-examination of this witness now. We can now bring in the next witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: The next witness, who attended on an earlier occasion, was granted measures of protection and was given the pseudonym letter E and is to enjoy the benefit of distortion of the facial image.

utterances.speaker: MR. GREAVES
utterances.text: Would Your Honours kindly give me leave to withdraw from the Court this afternoon and to do it as quietly as I can.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] You don't have to be quite that silent. You are entitled to have yourself treated, and you should know that as the co-chief of the Defence team, we have full confidence in Mr. Londrovic. Take care of yourself, Mr. Greaves, and we hope we will see you again tomorrow morning.

utterances.speaker: MR. GREAVES
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honours, for your very considerable consideration, and it's much appreciated by me.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Do you hear me, sir?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] First you are going to read the solemn declaration which is being given to you by the usher. Read it in your own language. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. Witness E, please be seated. First of all, we're going to ask you to verify your name on a piece of paper without, however, stating it. The usher will show you your name. Do not state your name. Simply nod if, in fact, it is your first and last name. [Witness complies] You are covered by protective measures. This is a closed session, and you can therefore speak without fear. You're protected within this Tribunal in this trial which has been initiated by the Prosecutor against Mr. Goran Jelisic. First you're going to answer the Prosecutor's questions, and tomorrow, most likely, you will answer the questions asked by Mr. Jelisic's Defence counsel. Mr. Nice, please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: I have provided the Court with bundles of summaries in English, French, and B/C/S. I'm sorry they weren't available earlier, but there have been difficulties, as you know, with the ordering of witnesses. If they could be distributed now, both to the Court and to the Defence, in whatever language would be most suitable, I would be grateful. If the usher -- I think the Defence would require some copies of the summaries in probably all languages, and if a copy in B/C/S could go to the witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Witness E, is the document you're looking at a summary in B/C/S that has been read by you; "Yes" or "No"?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS E
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Is it accurate, to the best of your knowledge and belief?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS E
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: May that therefore become an exhibit, with the English and French versions of it marked in a way that accords with the way similar documents have been marked in the past.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS E
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LONDROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] My apologies to both the Trial Chamber and to the learned colleague Mr. Nice, but I do not have a copy of the summary in B/C/S.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: This is Prosecution Exhibit 22, 22A for the French version and 22B for the B/C/S version.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Witness E, were you, on the 14th of May of 1992, arrested in Brcko and taken to the facility at Luka?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS E
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: You go there to the administration office, where you were questioned and where you surrendered your identification papers. Did you thereafter wait outside the office?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS E
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Did a car arrive?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS E
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Who was in the car?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS E
utterances.text: I didn't know his name until I came into his office, and his name was Adolf.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Before we come to that, my mistake. While outside the office, did you see something of a woman arriving?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS E
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: How did she arrive, on foot or in a vehicle?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS E
utterances.text: I just want to clarify which one. Adolf came, and also a woman came with him.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Yes, but before that, I want to deal with a woman who may have arrived separately and arrived as a detainee. Can you help with that woman, please?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS E
utterances.text: Yes, of course I can. This woman was brought in a red van. She was brought by Arkan's men. She was delivered into the building across from the hangar.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Could the witness please look first at our Exhibit 16, which can be placed on the ELMO. I'll hand to the usher another series of photographs which will become a subsequent exhibit in preparation, but let's look at this exhibit first.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Witness E, in order to preserve your facial anonymity, when I ask you to indicate something on the photograph, would you use the pointer that the usher will hand to you. Use the pointer. Stay in your seat, but point it out not on the screen but on the photograph that's to your right-hand side where the usher is indicating. If you look to your right, on there. Right. If you point something out there, then we can all see it. Do you see it? So where were you and where was the woman when she first arrived?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS E
utterances.text: It's on the right photograph [indicating]. It is, yes, a hangar, but there is no office, because that office was further to the right from this office that we can see.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Very well. Then the next photograph, which is going to become an exhibit, can conveniently -- if this doesn't offend the rules, if one version can be laid on the ELMO and the rest produced as exhibits. It saves the usher some time. This can become Exhibit 23, I think.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Yes, that is Prosecution Exhibit 23.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: When the woman arrived, does this photograph show where she went or where she waited?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS E
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Using the pointer, show us where, please.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS E
utterances.text: This is his office [indicating]. That is the entrance to his office [indicating], and the woman was here [indicating] and I was here [indicating].

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Sorry, where were you?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS E
utterances.text: Right here [indicating], next to this door here [indicating], leaning against a wall.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: What state was the woman in? What, if anything, was she saying?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS E
utterances.text: The woman was wearing a red sweater, a chequered skirt, and her hair was quite dishevelled, and she wore slippers on her feet.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Did she say anything?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS E
utterances.text: She was only shouting, crying out, "I am not guilty, I am not guilty, I have done nothing."

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Some minutes later, did another vehicle arrive?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS E
utterances.text: Yes, a black car. It reached the petrol station, entered about 10 metres inside, and stopped.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Who was in the car?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS E
utterances.text: I did not know his name before, but a man in police clothes came out, and a girl who was wearing a white dress, black stockings, a white dress with dots.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: The man, did he carry anything with him?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS E
utterances.text: Yes, he had a sawn-off rifle. It was about that size [indicating]. I did not know the name of that particular rifle. And this girl had a pistol in her hand.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: On arrival, did the man -- that is, the man, the man in the car -- did he speak to any other uniformed person present?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS E
utterances.text: No, that man in uniform was approached by this man with long hair, and said there was a balija woman, an SDA woman, there.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: The woman who had recently arrived, was she standing or sitting?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS E
utterances.text: Sitting.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: What did the man who had arrived, who was carrying the gun, then do?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS E
utterances.text: He walked in her direction and got her by the scruff of her neck with his left hand and drew her to one of his offices -- it could be right here [indicating] -- and made her fall, pushed her so she fell down against the kerb, and then he fired at the back of her head.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Where was her head -- precisely, if you can say -- in relation to any feature of the road or the gutter or the kerb?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS E
utterances.text: There is a kerb here [indicating], next to his office, and right next to the kerb, that is where he pushed her and killed her.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: When her head went down, did you see what her head was over when it went down?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS E
utterances.text: Well, as he fired, she just remained lying there.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: I meant what part of the road or the gutter, or whatever it was, was her head over --

utterances.speaker: WITNESS E
utterances.text: There, right on the kerb [indicating]. That's where she was, and then the one with the long hair shouted at us that we had to go in, that we had to move into the hangar.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Did you see that man, and the woman who had arrived with him, afterwards?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS E
utterances.text: With whom? The one in the police uniform killed her, and the one with the long hair pushed me and the other one who was detained with me, he pushed us into the hangar. It was a warehouse, as they called it, a warehouse. This one here [indicating]. That's where we entered.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Inside the hangar, were there other people present, or were you the only ones there?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS E
utterances.text: There were quite a number of people there.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Did the man and the long-haired girl or woman come into that hangar?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS E
utterances.text: The hairy one, the long-haired one, ordered us to enter. We entered, and to my right-hand side, in the hangar, there were quite a number of people. I was sitting here, across this door. That is, next to the railway tracks there is another door, and next to this door was a chair.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Did the man, the man in the police uniform, come into the hangar, and did he say something or did he do something?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS E
utterances.text: Yes. He entered the warehouse and fired into the ceiling.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Did he say anything or do anything at that time?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS E
utterances.text: No, at that moment, he was silent and fired at the hangar.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: The woman with whom he had arrived, was she with him?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS E
utterances.text: Yes, she was.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: What, if anything, did she have with her?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS E
utterances.text: She had a pistol in her hand.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: What did she do?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS E
utterances.text: Later on, she went from one man to the other asking for their full name. She reached me; I was sitting on the chair. She asked me what my first and last name was. I told her, and she aimed at me but then fired a bullet into the door right next by my head.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: At this time or at about this time, had the man in the police uniform been saying anything, or looking for any particular person, or anything like that?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS E
utterances.text: Nothing. He wasn't looking for anything. He went out. And as he was going out, another one, in a police uniform too, said that there was a Croat there who had raped a nine-year-old Serb girl. Adolf then approached him and kicked him in the head.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Just "Yes" or "No": Were you provided some food that evening?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS E
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: And after you were provided food, did you see the man in the police uniform again, either in the hangar or at the hangar door?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS E
utterances.text: In the hangar door, in the doorway.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: And was he the only person there in uniform, or was there somebody else there as well?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS E
utterances.text: He was wearing a police uniform, and that one with the long hair was in a multi-coloured uniform, and the others were wearing the old SMB -- Yugoslav, that is, People's Army uniforms.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: What happened on this occasion when you saw them?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS E
utterances.text: Nothing. But he left, and then they began distributing supper.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Was there a man present who'd been a male nurse at a hospital?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS E
utterances.text: He was the one who distributed food.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: What ultimately happened to him?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS E
