utterances.text: Ultimately, what happened to him is that a soldier -- rather a man in a police uniform came, took him out, and he was hitting him with his baton, and there were two men in the doorway, and also hit him in the chest. He fell and cried out, and meanwhile, I only heard a shot.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Did you see that man who had been male nurse again or not?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS E
utterances.text: No. No. No.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: At the time that he was called out, the man you've been referring to as Adolf, where was he?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS E
utterances.text: Outside.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Was this the only man who was called out of the warehouse or were there other people called out?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS E
utterances.text: Another one, also a male nurse, he was also taken out, and I could hear how they beat him. That same policeman hit him by the door, and when he would reach the door, the others would meet him with their feet and would kick him, and then, as he would come out of the door, one could hear a shot.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Any other detainees removed? So how many altogether?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS E
utterances.text: Eight, with me being the ninth.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: What happened to the total of eight? Was it the same as had happened to the earlier detainees or different?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS E
utterances.text: Same. Same. Also a shot, a scream, a shot, and the same policeman came up to me and told me -- I was wearing a yellow T-shirt, and he said, "You, yellow, you come with me."

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Just to conclude what you can help us with about those first eight people, did you see any of those alive again after the time when you heard shots?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS E
utterances.text: No. No.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: You, taken out at as the ninth, where were you taken?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS E
utterances.text: The policeman came after me and said, "Come, yellow guy, your turn. Stand up." I stood up, and he began to beat me with his baton. He ordered me to run. I was running, and he was hitting me. As I reached the door, all I could see, only how a foot came up and hit me in the chest. I fell, and they beat me and beat me and beat me. And the one with -- the long-haired guy, he pulled me by my hair and made me stand up, and he told me to enter. I started to where I had turned over my documents. I started towards this office, and he hit me, and he said, "Not there; over here." And I thought they wanted to kill me in the WC, so I started towards the toilet. I saw the door; I entered. They were sitting inside, nine of them.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Can you pause just for one minute. Remember, please, Witness E, that there are, of course, some people who are interpreting what you're saying into another language, and if you can try and go just a little bit more slowly, it'll make their jobs that much more easy.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS E
utterances.text: Sure.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Could you use the pointer and the photograph that's on the device on your right and show which doorway you went into when you were taken across the road? Does it show it here?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS E
utterances.text: That's the door [indicating]. That's the office.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: And when you went in there eventually, who was inside?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS E
utterances.text: There were troops, and the one in the police uniform, called Adolf, was sitting there, because they called him Adolf.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: When you say "they" called him Adolf, do you mean other people in this room? Or had you heard him called Adolf before then?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS E
utterances.text: The one with the long hair, he addressed him as Adolf, and that was when I heard that his name was Adolf.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: How many people altogether were there in this room?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS E
utterances.text: There were nine of them, and he was the tenth.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: What happened?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS E
utterances.text: When they brought me in, a young man was standing, dark T-shirt and camouflage trousers.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: What happened to you?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS E
utterances.text: The one in the black T-shirt asked Adolf, "Shall this one beat him or the one in the black T-shirt?" And Adolf answered, "You, Sasa. You hit him." And Sasa took gloves, put them on, and made me lean against a wardrobe and began to beat me. And he beat me and he beat me until he got me in the temple. As he hit me in the temple, I began to fall, and as I was falling, Adolf kicked me with his feet. I fell down on the floor, and all I felt was water pouring down my neck. So they took me back in. Adolf stood up and began to beat me. One young man from the corner then spoke up: "Adolf, don't beat him. It's a shame; he is a poor man." And Adolf said, "What do you mean, he's a poor man?" And he said, "Well, he carries things for other people, he drives, he does all sorts of chores for other people." And then Adolf stopped beating me and told me to go and wash the blood off my face. And I went and washed myself and came back. And then he ordered me to sit down next to him, and I sat down, and then he told me, "Nobody has left this room alive, but you are going home, and go and feed that child of yours and your wife." And then he wrote a pass for me.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: I may come to the pass in just a minute, but while you were sitting in the chair in the office, did somebody come into the office, one of the other men, and say something to Adolf?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS E
utterances.text: Yes. Yes. He did.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: What did you believe his name to be?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS E
utterances.text: Sok.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: What did you notice about his condition?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS E
utterances.text: His hands were bloody. And he told Adolf, "I did what you told me to do. I cut off his ears, his nose, and I gouged his eyes out. What do I do next with him?" And Adolf told him, "Go and kill him." And he said, "I will not kill him; I will slit his throat."

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Can we deal now with the pass? Tell us about the pass. You were given a pass?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS E
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: By whom?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS E
utterances.text: Adolf.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Will you look, please, at this document. It has an English translation attached to it, but I'm afraid not a French one, I think -- it may have French, actually.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: I have a copy in French, English, and Serbo-Croat.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: May it collectively, then, be Exhibit 24, or whatever it is. May the usher please --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please. Microphone for the counsel.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: I'm sorry about the microphone. Could the usher very kindly put an English version on the ELMO, with the witness having the original version from which to read -- sorry; I'm grateful to Mr. Tochilovsky. Can I have that back a moment? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: The English version has the name blanked out, and Witness E, you are, of course, not to mention your name at all, because you are a protected witness.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS E
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Looking, as you do, at the original version, is this a copy of the document that was provided to you?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS E
utterances.text: The one before me, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: And it purports to come from the Serb Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina, the Autonomous District of Semberija and Majevica, Brcko municipality. There is a number given, and a date, the 14th of May, and it reads --

utterances.speaker: WITNESS E
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: -- "Pursuant to the decision of the War Presidency of the Brcko Municipality," and then the decision's number is given. It says, "The following pass is issued," and it sets out your name and ID number. "Special allowing him to leave the war zone and the area of the Brcko municipality. This pass must be used exclusively with an identification card." It is then signed over an official stamp on the original: "War Presidency of the Brcko Municipality," signed "Adolf." Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS E
utterances.text: It is.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Did you see that document being signed, or not, or can't you remember?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS E
utterances.text: What do you mean, "signed"? This document he signed, and he wrote, and it was 100 per cent checked, and he gave it to me and told me that nobody will lay his finger on me; that whoever stopped me, all I had to do was show him this document. And I brought this document home.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: While you were in the office, was something said about an army major who had arrived at Luka?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS E
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Tell us about that.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS E
utterances.text: Sok entered and told Adolf that Major had arrived and said that the killing had to be stopped, and Adolf answered "I am here."

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Yes? Did he go on and say anything else? He said "I am here"; what did he mean by that?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS E
utterances.text: "If need be, I will also square the accounts with the whole army."

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: You were at Luka for what period of time, Witness E, altogether?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS E
utterances.text: Altogether, I was brought at 12, and that policeman, that lad who took me home, that Goran, he told Adolf, and it was that he would also be caught by the curfew, that he could not move around either, and the curfew was -- it means around 9.00 in the evening.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: You left Luka at what time?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS E
utterances.text: Well, when it -- if this Goran said that the curfew would be shortly, Adolf then said that we could go, and I and this Goran left, and he brought me home.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: So you were there for something under nine hours, but --

utterances.speaker: WITNESS E
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: -- most of the time that you were there, who appeared to be in control at Luka?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS E
utterances.text: In control in Luka? Adolf.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Was there anybody else who seemed to have authority superior to or authority over Adolf?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS E
utterances.text: No, no, because all of them, both Sok and Sasa and everybody else, addressed him and turned to him, to Adolf. There was nobody else responsible. Since he gave me the pass, then it was quite obvious who was in control. Adolf.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Did you get to know Adolf by any other name?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS E
utterances.text: I learned, when I escaped across both front lines and got to our territory where we were, then I learned from stories that that was that Goran Jelisic. But I knew him in Luka only as Adolf.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Answer the following question just "Yes" or "No", if you would, please.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS E
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: If you were to see this man again now, do you think you'd recognise him or not? Just "Yes" or "No".

utterances.speaker: WITNESS E
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Please look around this room and see if you can see the man Adolf.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS E
utterances.text: [Witness complies]

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: The witness identified the defendant.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Can you clear one thing up for us, in case there's any confusion? You also used the name "Goran", I think, in reference to the person who took you home.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS E
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Is that another person called -- well, is that person called Goran different from Adolf?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS E
utterances.text: Different, yes. It was a child, a young man, a boy. He couldn't have been more than 19. I knew him from the civilian life. That boy came from Grcica, and Adolf knows only too well who that was.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Going back to the first particular event that you told us about, the killing, by shooting, of the woman at the side of the road, who did that shooting?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS E
utterances.text: Adolf.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Your Honour, this witness, I think, has -- Your Honour, it hasn't been possible, for reasons of the substitution of witnesses, I think, for this witness to go through, in advance, the two lists of names. May I ask, and I hope it won't take a lot of time, that he can have those exhibits in front of him, and he can do the exercise in our presence. I see that's acceptable to Mr. Londrovic. While the exhibits are being produced, I'll explain the position to the witness. Witness E, you're going to be shown some lists of names, a longer list and then a shorter list. I want you just -- don't worry about what the lists are. Just look at the names, and if you come to a name that you recognise, tell us, and I shall then ask you whether you knew what happened to the man. Perhaps you could put them on the ELMO, please, on the ELMO. So take your time. It's a burden for you to do it in the presence of everyone else, but don't be alarmed. If you see a name that you recognise, just tell us, and then I'll ask you a supplementary question.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Tell us the name.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS E
utterances.text: Glavocevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Stipo Glavocevic, what do you know about him? What, if anything, do you know of his fate, of what happened to him?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS E
utterances.text: I don't know anything about him. I heard that he was killed. I just heard it from -- I can only confirm what I saw with my own eyes, what I saw with my own eyes, not through somebody else's eyes, and I know this --

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Witness E, we understand that, and it's very helpful of you to be precise. But you're allowed to tell us, in relation to the names on this list, what you have heard about them. So you heard of Stipo Glavocevic, that he was killed. Now, do you know anything about the other three names on that list? If not, we'll turn to the next sheet.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS E
utterances.text: I know Stipo Glavocevic and I know Suad Hadzic.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: What can you tell us about him? Do you know what happened to him, or had you heard what happened to him?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS E
utterances.text: I heard about it, but I wouldn't like to say it. I would prefer to just say what I saw with my own eyes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Well, as I've explained to you, you're allowed to tell us what you had heard, and perhaps you would tell us what you had heard about him.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS E
utterances.text: I heard that Stipo Glavocevic arrived at Luka with his ears and nose cut off, and Adolf asked around to other detainees to kill him and nobody wanted to, and then he killed him. I heard the same about Suad Hadzic, that he was killed in the health centre. So those were the stories. But I did not see it, so I cannot say that it was so, so I would prefer not to.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Your Honour, we know that we are doing this at the request of the Defence, and I hope I've set the witness's mind at rest that he can tell us what he has heard.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Perhaps you would have a look at the next sheet, please. If you would cast your eyes down this list of names, and if you see a name that you know something about, let us know.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS E
utterances.text: I don't know anyone among these.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Next sheet, please.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS E
utterances.text: Suljo Pezerovic, he was also killed at Luka.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Is that something you heard or something that you knew about directly?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS E
utterances.text: I heard about it.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS E
utterances.text: We heard about it when people came back from the camp.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Nobody else on that page?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS E
utterances.text: None, no one else.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Next sheet.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS E
utterances.text: Redenica.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: First name Rahim?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS E
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: What did you know of him?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS E
utterances.text: I also heard that he was killed too, again only heard and nothing more.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Whereabouts did you hear that he was killed?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS E
utterances.text: They said that he was killed in Es.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Thank you. Anybody else on that page that you recognise?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS E
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: The next sheet, I think the last on this longer list, a few names here.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS E
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: If you would very kindly look at another list which is rather shorter, tell us if there are any there whose names you recognise.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS E
utterances.text: Ahmet Hodzic, called Papa.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Yes. We can take this very briefly because we've heard a lot about him. What did you hear about him?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS E
utterances.text: I heard that he was killed. That is what I heard from those who were exchanged, and they told it. They told a lot about him, the most.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Any other names on that page?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS E
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: The next sheet, please.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS E
utterances.text: Kibe Becirevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: That's number 16, yes. What can you tell us about him?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS E
utterances.text: I also heard that he was killed.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Whereabouts was he killed?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS E
utterances.text: As according to them, he was killed in some bowling lanes. I don't know. This is what they were saying, so this is the story that I heard.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Any other names?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS E
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: The last sheet, please. A few more names.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS E
utterances.text: Osman Vatic was an attorney.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Did you hear what happened to him?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS E
utterances.text: For a long time, I did not hear, but then those who came, who were exchanged, came and said that he had been killed.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Any other names on that page?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS E
utterances.text: No, I don't know anyone else.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: That concludes my examination of this witness. I know that the Court will not be concluding his evidence today. He may need to be reminded that, of course, he's not able to contact the Prosecution at this stage.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Witness E, for reasons which must have been explained to you or which will be, you cannot be questioned this afternoon by Goran Jelisic's attorneys. You have to remain tonight. We regret that, because we know that represents great sacrifice to you, and I would like to take advantage of this time to thank you for having come here. Do not contact anybody, not anyone in the Defence or the Prosecution. Remain in your hotel or visit The Hague. You remain under protective measures, and the Witness and Victims Unit will take care of you. Tomorrow morning, I must tell you that we will resume at 9.00, and, at that time, you will be asked questions by the Defence and then possibly some further questions by the Prosecutor, after which you will have completed your assignment. We're going to have you escorted out of the courtroom. Once the witness has left, perhaps we can deal with the report, because I think we've had the time to talk about it, and we can further discuss it in order to save some time. We will close the blinds so that nobody can see your face or your features as you leave the courtroom.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Nice, Mr. Londrovic, we have reviewed the report, specifically, paragraph 9 or, rather, chapter 9, which must also relate to the next-to-the-last paragraph of chapter 11. Paragraph 9, let me remind you for those who don't have it in front of them, it's called, "The Demolition," and it says, "I frequently observed polygon-shaped sectors in the shapes of the Bosnian mosques, but I've never noticed any of this type of structure in non-religious buildings." Under 11, which is the final summary of the report, not counting the annexes, in the next-to-the-last paragraph, he's more categorical. He says, "One part --" the expert is more categorical, and he says, "One part of those stones came from the demolition of a mosque." What we need to know is whether we need to bring the Australian expert in to the court in respect of this chapter 9. Perhaps the following position could be taken: Either the Prosecutor decides not to use chapter 9, as it stands, or the expert could change his opinions. I'm not here to ask him to do so, but if necessary, we'll have to call in the Australian expert, who can then be subject to a cross-examination on chapter 9. It seems to me, though, in agreement with my colleagues, that's what we might do. That's the only solution we could have, unless we set up a video-link conference. But despite any pleasure that our registrar would have about going to Australia, he's gone to Zagreb, but I don't think that would be very good for the finances of the Tribunal. For that reason, I turn both to the Defence and to the Prosecution. Could you reach an agreement? Mr. Nice, you are the one who has brought in this evaluation.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: The reason I raise it at this stage was because Mr. Greaves had indicated to me that objection was taken not to the factual findings of the expert, and indeed it would be surprising if the expert was making up what he describes there, but to his conclusions. If you would be good enough to turn to the photographs, which you may not have them in the French version, let me just check -- I see you don't have the photographs, but you may have them in the English version. In any event, I can make mine available comparatively swiftly. There are two photographs reflecting what he found.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: I have the English version, and, incidentally, page 10 is missing, which is a crucial page.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Yes. It's only missing in Your Honour's copy. I'm sorry about that. I don't know how that came about, and I know that Your Honour will have been able to read the version in French of page 10, and it's a photocopying error for which I apologise.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: If you have it, it's all right.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Does the English version have the photographs attached to it?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: Yes, it has.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Photographs 10 and 12 are the -- photograph 10 --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: We have got photo 2. Wait a second.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Photograph 10 is the piece of masonry with the obtuse angle, 145 degrees, from which the witness draws a certain inference, and photograph 12 is the tombstone inscribed in Arabic. Now, if the Court would be good enough to go back to paragraph or chapter 9, we can partition out what he says into factual findings and expert opinion. As I understand it, the Defence objection is taken to the ability of this witness to speak as an expert. His factual findings start off, at the beginning of chapter 9, with the things that he found, and that's a factual finding; the five main components of the rubble; the bricks in their thousands; the tiles; the broken cement blocks; the dressed masonry blocks, and the clay. He then goes on to say that the dressed masonry blocks indicate that at least some of the demolition rubble comes from demolished mosque or mosques. He bases this on the conclusion about the angles "we measured on the faces of the dressed blocks, photograph 10", saying that precise measurement of the angles is not possible, but approximately-recorded estimates done in the field were 145 degrees. He then says, "If the true angles were, in fact, 144 degrees, then the blocks could have come from a ten-sided polygonal structure." That paragraph contains something in the nature of a conclusion in the first sentence and, indeed, an explanation from the conclusion in the second, but the balance of it is a factual finding. The next paragraph, where he says he has frequently seen polygonal structures forming minarets of mosques in Bosnia, but has never seen such polygonal structures in secular architecture, is also factual. It speaks of his experience, as does the following paragraph which deals with the finding of bricks, similar to the type described, cemented to the inside of a demolished minaret. What follows thereafter is his observations and conclusions, which also extends to the conclusion about photograph 12. If my understanding of the Defence objection, outlined by Mr. Greaves before he fell sick, is correct, then the objection is to the conclusion but not to the factual findings. I think that it would not be a justifiable expenditure of money to call this witness from Australia to give, by way of a conclusion, what is little more, it may be thought, than a practical or common-sense conclusion that many people could draw from the factual findings that he makes. Accordingly, providing the facts go in, that is, the material that he found, along with the measurement of the angles and a reflection of his own experience, then I'm happy not to have read out, as part of the fundamental record of this case, his conclusions. But if it's being challenged that he found the things that he said he found, or that indeed his experience in relation to such commonplace events as he describes thereafter was as it is, then it might be necessary for him to be called, for it is quite important to know what items were found included in the rubble that covered this mass grave. Now, of course, Mr. Londrovic may well have been allocating this part of an argument on exclusion to Mr. Greaves and may not, for all I know, have discussed the basis of their objection in detail, and I understand the difficulties of communication that he and Mr. Greaves have. But I was certainly told that there was objection to the expertise of the witness. I was not told that there was any objection to his factual findings. So that's as far as I can take it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Londrovic?

utterances.speaker: MR. LONDROVIC
utterances.text: Your Honours, my learned colleague, Michael Greaves, offered a compromise to the Prosecution. If they were to omit paragraph 9, the expert would not be required to come here. However, if they decline to do so, I see no other way but to call the witness and have him cross-examined here.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Which means that you really don't agree with anything. Let's not try to hide the facts as they are. Let's be clear. We're talking about chapter 9 here, and it's the important one. I do not think -- well, at the very most, we could have asked the expert to come to speak about his conclusions. But if one reads it carefully, it says that part of the stones came from the demolition of mosques, and he is affirmative there, but he also said this in chapter 9. Are you prepared to give up chapter 9 of the report, Mr. Nice?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: I'm certainly not at present prepared to give up chapter 9 in its entirety, because, as I have indicated, partitioning out facts from conclusion of the facts should be noncontentious, in my submission, and may be of value to the Chamber, using its own powers of deduction and sense, without the need for any expertise or purported expertise. It may be that I can produce evidence from the OTP investigators who accompanied this field inspection of the finding of the polygonal structures and the Arabic-inscribed tombstone that will substitute for the findings of this witness. But nevertheless, it would be sensible, frankly, if the factual findings are not truly in dispute, for them to go before you, unchallenged, but without any expression of opinion. That's the compromise I'm happy to make. I'm not in the position to bargain pieces of evidence in or out; that's not my function here. I am here to ensure that the procedures aren't overwasteful.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] What is factual and what isn't? I think that's the problem; that's the question. I understand, and my colleagues have suggested that I reach the same conclusion, but I would like you to explain what is factual and what isn't, because what the Defence is challenging is in fact what is factual. The masonry blocks -- look at page 12. The masonry blocks which were dressed at least show that some of these stones come from the demolition of one or several mosques. I believe that you consider that this is factual; is that correct, Mr. Nice?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: I think, to be strictly accurate, the factual parts, as I indicated a little earlier, are what he found, and indeed the measurements, the angular measurements of what he found, and also factual is his saying, "I have frequently seen polygonal structures forming minarets of mosques but have never seen polygonal structures in secular architecture." That is factual. Similarly, his saying that he's seen bricks of the type described in mosques is factual, but the balance is, I think, inference, deduction, or opinion. So I would wish him to able to say what he found and what his experience was and then leave deductions, of course, for the Court.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Nice, you consider that he is mentioning or he is referring to where these stones would come from; that's factual, or that's a matter of opinion?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: That's a matter of opinion.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: A matter of opinion?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Well, it's a fine distinction, but it's a proper distinction to say, "I have seen bricks like this in mosques. I find bricks like this in the ground."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: [Interpretation] This is factual?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Both of those observations are factual. It would be for the Tribunal of fact, in absence of expert opinion, to say, "Those two pieces of evidence satisfy us that the bricks in the ground came from a mosque."

utterances.speaker: MR. LONDROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I do beg your pardon, Your Honours, but before I conclude --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We have not finished with the discussion. Just a moment. Excuse me. Excuse me. Let me first give the floor to Judge Rodrigues.

utterances.speaker: MR. LONDROVIC
utterances.text: I realise that this is not the end, but if I may, perhaps it will be of some help to my learned friend.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Excuse me. I would first like Judge Rodrigues to be able to ask his questions, if you don't mind. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I would like to address my question to Mr. Londrovic. I am on page 12 of the report. I don't know whether the various versions correspond in terms of the pagination, but in any case, paragraph 9, which is called "Demolition Stones," in paragraph 3 of that, there is a description of -- and I think we all agree with that when we say that's a fact. And afterwards, in paragraph -- let me see -- paragraphs 5 and 6, one also finds a description which is totally factual. There is no opinion given there. That is paragraphs 5 and 6. They refer to cement blocks and masonry blocks. I believe there is no opinion; this is simply factual. Is the Defence also contesting this description of the witness?

utterances.speaker: MR. LONDROVIC
utterances.text: Your Honours, I now find myself in a very embarrassing situation, because I received the B/C/S version of this report about an hour ago; there are no photographs here. I did manage to find what you have been referring to, Your Honour, but our principle objection is -- and I really do not understand the insistence on this part, because Mr. Jelisic is not charged with the demolition of mosques. Under Count 1, the period covered by Count 1 is May 1992. At that time, the mosques in Brcko were still standing up. And finally, Mr. Jelisic certainly was not the one who demolished them. The principal objection of the Defence to this document is that this expert is not an expert on building materials. As far as I could see, he is an anthropologist. And he nevertheless draws certain conclusions, makes certain conclusions about the types of building materials he found in that mass grave.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. Londrovic. Was that the comment that you wanted to make?

utterances.speaker: MR. LONDROVIC
utterances.text: Yes. And may I add only one thing: I'm sorry, the Defence are constantly being asked to yield in to the Prosecution, but we have been doing it really as much as we could, and we were also proposing to the Prosecution methods whereby we could do this much more expediently. However, we were not met with the understanding by the Prosecution, and I think that most probably on Monday, or at a later stage, I will also make certain objections regarding the work of the gentleman from the Prosecution, because we do have an agreement on facts, and as far as I could see, in the examination-in-chief, they're beginning to violate that agreement on the procedure. But if they continue doing so, then we shall object to the methods used by the Prosecution, and it will be up to Their Honours to decide whether the Defence is right or wrong.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] This kind of announcement, if you have something to say, let's take advantage of the time that was given to the Defence to make its comment, but not to wait until next Monday. That seems a little strange to me, but next Monday, I can tell you right now, I'm going to have some things to say about what you say. Just say it. Just say it. But that isn't --

utterances.speaker: MR. LONDROVIC
utterances.text: Well, you see, I'm expecting the Prosecution to behave like gentlemen. They know what it says on the agreement on facts, and I know that the Prosecutors in the West are gentlemen, even though I do not have much experience. My --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I cannot accept this type of remark. I would like that remark to be withdrawn. Up to this point, if, here, there have been any people who are qualified to make comments, whether lawyers or legal specialists are acting as gentlemen, that is for the Judges to do so. At this point I do not allow you to make comments of this nature. Today, this is the first time that you're speaking, and I do not authorise you to make that type of judgement; only the Judges can say it, what point this or that legal specialist, whether that specialist from the Prosecution or the Defence is in contempt of the Tribunal. I do not accept that, and I ask that that comment be withdrawn. Do you withdraw it, or do you not?

utterances.speaker: MR. LONDROVIC
utterances.text: I withdraw it. No problem. I apologise if I offended the Court in this manner.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, we won't talk about that any more. Let's go back to the report. I would like to reach an agreement here. Possibly -- let me turn to Mr. Nice. Might it be possible that with the Defence, you could try, starting with Judge Rodrigues's comments, that is, up to the paragraph which speaks about mixed clay, that is, before the dressed masonry blocks and going to the end of paragraph 10, and including part of the stones came from the demolition of mosques, which we find in the summary, could you reach some type of wording about which you could call the Australian expert to ask whether he would agree with a certain type of redacting in order to make a distinction between what is factual and what is not, that is, to establish a criterion for that? As regards what is factual, these are the angles, the 145-degree angles. What is factual is his comment regarding the polygonal structure in the architecture of the minarets, when he said that he frequently saw structures in polygonal form in minarets. Mr. Londrovic, he may not be a specialist of mosques, but he is an anthropologist, and I point out to you, Mr. Londrovic, that an anthropologist is a category of scientists who carry out what would be called anthropology, that is, the science of civilisations. And in the science of civilisations and their origins, there are comments made about the buildings. But might we find some way of writing this which would not be one that you would substitute for that of the expert? Only the expert can do his own work, but you might telephone him and ask him whether he might be prepared to nuance his comments, and that would permit you to reach an agreement between the Prosecution and the Defence. That would be gentlemanly, Mr. Londrovic, that is, to reach a consensus. But, Mr. Londrovic, if the Australian expert must be brought in, we will do so. But the Judges in this Trial Chamber -- and I said it the first day -- their first concern is to ensure that this trial is completed within a reasonable amount of time, and I suppose that is in the interest, as well, of your client, that is, the accused. Therefore, that is what we are seeking to achieve. Mr. Nice, do you think that you could, with Mr. Londrovic and Mr. Greaves, speak with one another and see what can be changed on the basis of the criteria set by Judges Rodrigues and Riad, that is, the difference between what is only factual, and, of course, to submit this to the Australian expert. If there is no agreement, Mr. Londrovic, I can reassure you immediately, we will have the Australian expert brought in. But you should know that the Tribunal's budget can deal with that; that's not the issue. But it's not only a question of money; it's also a question of demonstrating that in this Tribunal, one can reach agreements. Not everything has to be done in the form of examinations-in-chief and cross-examinations. These are very ponderous procedures. But if nobody wants to -- it is not the Judge speaking to you. I don't come from the same system as you do, and therefore we will bring in the Australian expert. I want that to be very clear. The Judges will call in the Australian expert if that is necessary, but we're trying to see if we can find another solution. Mr. Prosecutor, can you try, on the basis of the distinction which I have just made, to do what I suggested?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Indeed, that's what I hoped from the beginning I could achieve, once I discovered that there was an objection to the alleged expertise expressed in the report. Maybe it will be easier for me to accomplish this with Mr. Greaves tomorrow. I'll do my best.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Fourmy, you can participate in this discussion. It doesn't seem difficult to ask the expert to modify his report, because the first one concerned, he, himself, can find it appropriate to nuance an opinion that he gave, especially since that appears in his report. And I could say that I am mindful of the fact that I have brought in an opinion here, and I am prepared to withdraw this opinion; I don't think this is completely impossible. But if not, I invite you to try to come to an agreement. If there is no agreement, well, then, I believe we will bring in the Australian expert. Mr. Londrovic? No further comments?

utterances.speaker: MR. LONDROVIC
utterances.text: Your Honours, the Defence will do its utmost to reach a compromise with the Prosecutor's office if that is at all possible. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. The Court stands adjourned. We will resume tomorrow at 9.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: 5.20 p.m., to be reconvened on Friday, the 3rd day of September, 1999, at 9.00 a.m. 21 22 23 24 25
